meta.reason: This session could not read any source. The shared WebSearch budget for the turn (200 calls) was used up before this agent ran, and WebFetch rejected every official URL tried (law.cornell.edu, uscode.house.gov, govinfo.gov, ecfr.gov, uscourts.gov, law.justia.com) as not on the allowlist. As the brief requires, every record has status 'unverifiable', days=null and source_url=null. The proposed corrections are in proposed_days / rule / trigger / assessment and come from the agent's own knowledge of the rules. Each one must be confirmed against suggested_source_url before it ships.
meta.amendments_note: No known Dec. 1, 2025 FRCP, FRAP or Criminal Rules amendment changes any day count listed here (the 2025 FRCP changes to Rules 16(b)(3) and 26(f)(3) add privilege-log content, not timing). Amendments taking effect Dec. 1, 2026 were not checked this session.

rules.note: You have 21 days after being served to answer or file a Rule 12(b) motion. If you returned a waiver of service, it is 60 days after the waiver request was sent (90 if sent outside the US). The United States and its officers or employees get 60 days.
rules.issue: The 21-day figure is right, but the app has no 60-day waiver branch and no 60-day United States branch, and addDays() does not move a due date that falls on a weekend or holiday to the next court day as Rule 6(a)(1)(C) requires.

rules.trigger: outer bound: 21 days before the scheduling order is due (that order is due by the earlier of 90 days after any defendant is served or 60 days after any defendant appears)
rules.note: The parties must hold the Rule 26(f) conference as soon as practicable and at least 21 days before the scheduling conference or the date the scheduling order is due. That is at most 69 days after the first defendant is served, or 39 days after the first appearance, whichever comes first.
rules.issue: Rule 26(f) does not require a conference 21 days after service. The 21 days count backwards from the Rule 16(b) scheduling-order date. Cases exempt under Rule 26(a)(1)(B), and courts that order otherwise, do not follow this timing.

rules.trigger: date of the Rule 26(f) conference (not the service date)
rules.note: Initial disclosures are due 14 days after the Rule 26(f) conference, unless the parties stipulate otherwise, the court orders otherwise, or a party objects at the conference.
rules.issue: 35 days after service has no basis in the rule. The deadline is triggered by the 26(f) conference date.

rules.trigger: earlier of 90 days after any defendant is served or 60 days after any defendant appears
rules.note: The judge must issue the scheduling order as soon as practicable, and no later than the earlier of 90 days after any defendant is served or 60 days after any defendant appears, unless the judge finds good cause for delay.
rules.issue: This deadline binds the court, not the parties. The app also ignores the 60-days-after-appearance alternative, which can be earlier.

rules.rule: Set by the scheduling order (Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(A)) and local rules; no FRCP default
rules.note: No federal rule sets a date for the close of discovery. The judge sets it in the scheduling order.
rules.issue: Showing a 120-day figure with the citation 'FRCP 26' presents an invented default as if it were a rule. Remove it, or make it a user-entered date from the scheduling order.

rules.trigger: trial date, or the date the case is to be ready for trial (count backwards); applies only absent a stipulation or court order
rules.note: Unless the parties stipulate or the court orders otherwise, expert disclosures are due at least 90 days before the trial date.
rules.issue: The 90 days count backwards from trial, not forward from service. In practice the scheduling order usually sets this date.

rules.note: Expert evidence offered only to contradict or rebut the other side's expert is due within 30 days after that party's disclosure, unless a stipulation or order says otherwise.
rules.issue: 120 days after service is wrong. The trigger is the opposing party's disclosure.

rules.trigger: close of all discovery; applies only when no local rule or court order sets another time
rules.note: Unless a local rule or court order sets a different time, a summary-judgment motion may be filed at any time until 30 days after all discovery closes. Most scheduling orders set their own dispositive-motion deadline.
rules.issue: 150 days after service, cited as 'Local Rules', is invented. The rule default is 30 days after the close of discovery, and the scheduling order usually controls.

rules.note: Unless the court orders otherwise, pretrial disclosures are due at least 30 days before trial. Objections are due within 14 days after the disclosures are made.
rules.issue: 210 days after service is invented. The deadline counts back from the trial date.

rules.trigger: entry of judgment (or, if the motion addresses a jury issue not decided by a verdict, the date the jury was discharged)
rules.note: A renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law is due no later than 28 days after entry of judgment. The court cannot extend this deadline (Rule 6(b)(2)).
rules.issue: The title uses the obsolete name 'JNOV'. The day count is correct.

rules.note: A motion for a new trial is due no later than 28 days after entry of judgment, and the court cannot extend it.
A motion to alter or amend a judgment is due no later than 28 days after entry of judgment, and the court cannot extend it.

rules.trigger: entry of the judgment or order appealed from
rules.note: A notice of appeal in a civil case is due within 30 days after the judgment or order is entered. A timely Rule 50(b), 52(b), 59 or certain Rule 54 or 60 motion resets this clock (FRAP 4(a)(4)).
rules.issue: The tolling effect of post-judgment motions under FRAP 4(a)(4) is not modeled.

rules.trigger: entry of the judgment or order appealed from
rules.note: When the United States, a federal agency, or a federal officer or employee (sued in an official capacity, or individually for acts tied to their duties) is a party, every party gets 60 days to file a notice of appeal.
rules.issue: The title 'US Gov Party' could suggest only the government gets 60 days. In fact any party in the case gets 60 days.

rules.rule: Local rule (Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(d)(1) sets no filing deadline); attorney's fees motion: Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(d)(2)(B)(i), 14 days
rules.note: Rule 54(d)(1) sets no deadline for filing a bill of costs; local rules do. A motion for attorney's fees is due 14 days after entry of judgment unless a statute or court order says otherwise.
rules.issue: The 14-day figure belongs to the attorney's-fees rule, Rule 54(d)(2)(B). It is not a deadline for a bill of costs under Rule 54(d)(1).

rules.rule: No fixed deadline: Fed. R. Crim. P. 10 governs procedure only; initial appearance is 'without unnecessary delay' under Fed. R. Crim. P. 5(a)(1)(A)
rules.trigger: arrest (initial appearance); arraignment is scheduled by the court
rules.note: Federal rules set no number of days for arraignment. After arrest, a person must be brought before a magistrate judge without unnecessary delay. For warrantless arrests, the Constitution generally requires a probable-cause decision within 48 hours (County of Riverside v. McLaughlin, 500 U.S. 44 (1991)). State deadlines vary by state.
rules.issue: '3 business days, Fed. R. Crim. P. 10' is invented. Rule 10 sets no time limit, and the 48-hour McLaughlin rule is a constitutional standard, not a rule-based deadline.

rules.rule: 18 U.S.C. § 3142(f) (Bail Reform Act); not Fed. R. Crim. P. 46
rules.note: In federal court, a detention hearing is held immediately at the first appearance. It can be postponed up to 5 days at the defendant's request or 3 days at the government's, not counting weekends and legal holidays. State bail timing varies.
rules.issue: The wrong authority is cited (Rule 46), and the trigger is wrong. The statute counts from the first appearance, not one day from arrest.

rules.trigger: initial appearance (not arrest); 14 days if in custody, 21 days if not
rules.note: A federal preliminary hearing must be held within 14 days after the initial appearance if you are in custody, or 21 days if you are not. No hearing is held if you are indicted first. The deadline can be extended (Rule 5.1(d)).
rules.issue: The trigger is wrong (arrest instead of initial appearance), and the 21-day out-of-custody period is missing. Rule 5.1 does not distinguish felonies from misdemeanors.

rules.note: Federal rules have no separate 10-day misdemeanor period. If a preliminary hearing is required, it uses the same 14 or 21 days. Under Rule 5.1(a)(4), a defendant charged with a misdemeanor who consents to trial before a magistrate judge gets no preliminary hearing.
rules.issue: The 10-day misdemeanor period is invented; it may be a leftover from the pre-2009 10/20-day rule.

rules.trigger: later of: filing (and making public) of the indictment or information, or the defendant's first appearance before a judicial officer of the charging court
rules.note: In federal cases, trial must start within 70 days after the later of the indictment or information or the first court appearance, not counting excludable delays under § 3161(h). State speedy-trial limits are different.
rules.issue: The trigger is wrong (arrest), and the clock ignores excludable time, so the computed date is not a real deadline. The Act applies only to federal prosecutions.

rules.trigger: arrest or service of summons on the federal charge
rules.note: In federal cases, an indictment or information must be filed within 30 days of arrest or service of a summons on that charge. In a felony case, if no grand jury has been in session, the period is extended by 30 more days.
rules.issue: The citation is wrong: Rule 7 governs the form of an indictment, not its timing. The day count is right only for federal cases.

rules.trigger: later of entry of the criminal judgment (entered after sentencing) or the government's notice of appeal
rules.note: A federal criminal defendant must file a notice of appeal within 14 days after the judgment is entered, which happens after sentencing, not at the verdict. The court may extend this by up to 30 more days for excusable neglect or good cause (FRAP 4(b)(4)).
rules.issue: The trigger 'conviction_date' is wrong. A guilty verdict or plea is not the entry of judgment, so counting from it gives a date that is too early.

rules.trigger: later of entry of the judgment or order, or the filing of a notice of appeal by any defendant
rules.note: When the government is allowed to appeal, it has 30 days.
rules.issue: Same trigger problem as crim_appeal_fed: it should count from entry of judgment, not the conviction date.

rules.trigger: latest of: the date the judgment of conviction becomes final; removal of a government-created impediment; a newly recognized retroactive right; or discovery of new facts
rules.note: A federal prisoner has one year, usually counted from the date the conviction becomes final. With no appeal, that is when the 14-day appeal period ends. If there was an appeal but no certiorari petition, it is 90 days after the court of appeals' judgment (Clay v. United States, 537 U.S. 522 (2003)).
rules.issue: The limit is one year (anniversary date), not 365 days counted from the conviction date. The trigger is wrong and can produce a date that is too early or too late.

rules.trigger: date the state judgment becomes final at the end of direct review (or when the time to seek review expires), tolled while a properly filed state post-conviction application is pending
rules.note: A state prisoner has one year from the date the state conviction becomes final to file a federal habeas petition. The clock pauses while a properly filed state post-conviction case is pending.
rules.issue: § 2244(d) applies only to state prisoners, yet it is placed in a rule set alongside federal appeal rules. It counts 365 days from the conviction date and ignores the finality trigger and statutory tolling.

rules.note: Federal criminal appeal: 14 days after entry of judgment.

rules.note: The deadline to appeal a state conviction depends on the state; many use 30 days, but California felony appeals get 60.

rules.note: The court sets the deadline for a motion to suppress. In federal court, if no deadline is set, it is the start of trial.

rules.note: 21 days after service in federal court (60 if service was waived or the United States is the defendant).

rules.note: The judge sets the close of discovery.

rules.note: 30 days after judgment (60 if a federal party is in the case).

rules.rule: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 borrows the forum state's personal-injury limitations period (Wilson v. Garcia, 471 U.S. 261 (1985); Owens v. Okure, 488 U.S. 235 (1989))

rules.rule: SEC Enforcement Manual practice (no statute or rule)

rules.rule: State law (e.g., Cal. Fam. Code § 242: hearing within 21 days, or 25 for good cause, of the TRO)

rules.note: The time to respond to a family-law petition depends on the state.

rules.trigger: the immigration judge's oral decision, or the mailing or electronic service of a written decision; the notice must be RECEIVED by the BIA within 30 calendar days
rules.note: An appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals must be received by the BIA within 30 calendar days after the judge's decision. If the last day falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.
rules.issue: The 'received, not mailed' requirement is not shown. It also needs confirmation that no 2025–2026 EOIR rule shortened this period; that could not be checked this session.

rules.note: The immigration court sets hearing dates.
rules.issue: 90 days is invented.

rules.trigger: date of the final order of removal (usually the BIA decision)
rules.note: A petition for review must be filed in the court of appeals within 30 days after the final removal order. Filing it does not automatically stop removal; a separate stay motion is needed.
rules.issue: The note should not call the deadline jurisdictional; the Supreme Court addressed its nature in Riley v. Bondi (2025), which still needs to be read and confirmed.

rules.rule: State civil-procedure rules (e.g., Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 412.20: 30 days); federal 21 days

rules.trigger: entry of judgment, or denial of discretionary review by the state court of last resort (not the mandate); a timely rehearing petition resets the clock
rules.note: A certiorari petition is due within 90 days after judgment, or after the state high court denies review.

rules.trigger: date the conviction becomes final (plus statutory triggers and tolling)
rules.note: The limit is one year from the date the conviction becomes final, not 365 days from the conviction.
rules.issue: The two statutes are combined, and 365 days is used instead of one year.

rules.rule: Art. 32, UCMJ (10 U.S.C. § 832); R.C.M. 405; no fixed day count

rules.note: An accused service member must be arraigned within 120 days of charges being preferred or restraint being imposed, minus excluded periods.

rules.issue: This is California-specific and is presented as general.

rules.trigger: date the child entered foster care; then every 6 months
rules.note: For children in foster care, federal law requires a case review at least every 6 months.
rules.issue: This applies to dependency (child-welfare) cases, not delinquency, and the trigger is not stated.

rules.trigger: date the child entered foster care (the earlier of the abuse or neglect finding or 60 days after removal); then every 12 months
rules.note: A permanency hearing is required within 12 months after a child enters foster care and every 12 months after that.
rules.issue: Dependency only. The 'entered foster care' trigger is defined in § 675(5)(F).

other_findings.original: Calendar days added with no weekend or holiday roll-forward; business days skip only Saturday and Sunday
other_findings.corrected: Apply Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1)(C) and Fed. R. Crim. P. 45(a)(1)(C): if the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, the deadline runs to the next court day. Exclude legal holidays (Rule 6(a)(6), 5 U.S.C. § 6103) from business-day counts, add 3 days for mail service (Rule 6(d)), and support counting backwards for 'before trial' deadlines.
other_findings.authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a), 6(d); Fed. R. Crim. P. 45(a), 45(c)

other_findings.corrected: Rule 12(a)(4)(A) gives 14 days to serve a responsive pleading after the court DENIES or postpones a Rule 12 motion. The time to oppose a motion is set by local rule.

other_findings.original: Summary judgment response: 21 days (local rules vary)
other_findings.corrected: The FRCP sets no response deadline; it is set by local rule or court order.

other_findings.original: 'State (Criminal)' heading over federal rules; 'Preliminary hearing: 14 days (felony) / 10 days (misdemeanor)'; 'Notice of appeal: 30 days (most states)'
other_findings.corrected: These are federal rules (Fed. R. Crim. P. 5.1(c): 14 days in custody / 21 days out of custody after the initial appearance). State deadlines vary and need per-state rule sets.

other_findings.original: clock_start is documented as 'date asylum application filed'; the 1-year bar is computed as elapsed > 365 days since clock_start minus paused_days
other_findings.corrected: The 1-year asylum filing deadline runs from the date of LAST ARRIVAL in the US, and it does not pause. Pausing applies only to the separate EAD clock, which counts from the filing date. Compute the bar from a separate last_arrival_date by calendar anniversary, and note the exceptions for changed or extraordinary circumstances and the exemption for unaccompanied children.
Use the one-year anniversary of the last arrival, not > 365 days, since leap years shift the count. Treat the result as 'deadline passed: an exception must be shown', not as an absolute bar.

other_findings.original: 180 days for EAD eligibility, counted from filing_date with no clock stoppage
other_findings.corrected: An asylum applicant may file for an EAD once 150 days have passed on the asylum EAD clock, and it cannot be granted before 180 days. Delays caused by the applicant stop the clock. Confirm whether Pub. L. 119-21 (2025) or any later DHS rule changed the EAD clock or validity period; that could not be checked this session.

other_findings.original: Accepts up to 365 days; 'Failure to depart ... results in a 10-year bar to re-entry and a civil penalty of $1,000–$5,000.'
other_findings.corrected: Voluntary departure granted before proceedings end is capped at 120 days, and at the end of proceedings at 60 days. Failing to depart brings a civil penalty of $1,000–$5,000 (the presumptive amount is $3,000) and 10 years of ineligibility for voluntary departure, cancellation of removal, adjustment of status, change of status and registry. The alternate removal order also takes effect, which can trigger separate inadmissibility bars. Filing a petition for review ends the grant.

other_findings.original: 'automatic 10-year bar + bond forfeiture'; '10-year re-entry bar now active'
other_findings.corrected: Use the same corrected consequences as immigration.js. The 10-year consequence is ineligibility for listed forms of relief under § 1229c(d)(1)(B), not a re-entry bar as such. Any re-entry bar comes from the removal order under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(9)(A). The § 1229c(d)(2) exception for abuse victims applies.

other_findings.original: Must apply within 1 year of entry
other_findings.corrected: Must apply within 1 year after the date of LAST arrival in the US, unless changed or extraordinary circumstances apply. Unaccompanied children are exempt.

other_findings.original: § 922(g)(8) ... TROs routinely require surrender within 24-72 hours — federal crime to miss
other_findings.corrected: § 922(g)(8) covers only protective orders issued after a hearing of which the person had actual notice and an opportunity to participate. Ex parte TROs do not qualify. Surrender deadlines come from state law.

The rule is correct in substance (Convention Art. 12). The trigger is the date of wrongful removal OR retention, and retention can be later than removal. No equitable tolling (Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez, 572 U.S. 1 (2014)). After 1 year, return is still ordered unless the child is shown to be settled.
other_findings.authority: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, Art. 12; 22 U.S.C. § 9003

other_findings.corrected: The rule is correct in substance: a defendant may file in court after the earlier of exhausting BOP administrative appeals or 30 days from the WARDEN'S RECEIPT of the request. Label the input as the receipt date.

other_findings.original: Federal — 14 days from judgment. Most states — 30 days. Missing this deadline permanently waives appellate rights.
other_findings.corrected: Federal: 14 days after entry of judgment (FRAP 4(b)(1)(A)); the district court may extend up to 30 days for excusable neglect or good cause (FRAP 4(b)(4)). State deadlines vary (for example, 60 days for California felony appeals). Missing the deadline can forfeit the appeal, so act immediately.
other_findings.authority: Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)(1)(A), 4(b)(4); Cal. Rules of Court 8.308(a)

other_findings.original: Federal habeas: 1-year statute of limitations from conviction becoming final (AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254/2255). State exhaustion required before federal filing.
other_findings.corrected: State prisoners: 1 year under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(d), tolled while a properly filed state post-conviction case is pending; state remedies must be exhausted first (§ 2254(b)). Federal prisoners: 1 year under § 2255(f), with no exhaustion requirement.

A general court-martial may adjudge any punishment the UCMJ and Manual allow for the offense, up to death where authorized. A special court-martial is capped at 12 months' confinement (6 months for a judge-alone special court-martial).

other_findings.original: tro_hearing_due = filed + 3 business days; protective_order_due = filed + 21 days
other_findings.corrected: Neither figure is a general rule. Let the user enter the hearing date shown on the TRO; e.g., Cal. Fam. Code § 242 sets 21 days, or 25 for good cause.
